content.thinking:
I'm designing a kraken rising from water in an Overwatch-style aesthetic—polished stylized sci-fi with clean bold shapes, bevels, and panel lines, picking a deep navy/teal palette with a strong accent color for the tentacled beast.

I'll add a simple splash base at the root — a lathed water mound with teal foam rings and a few droplet spheres, attached to the pelvis joint. For the skeleton, I'm planning a root "body" joint around y=1.2 with a spine chain rising into the mantle (tilted back) and a head/funnel section facing +Z, with tentacles reaching outward and down toward the water base.

For the limbs, I'm sketching 8 tentacles radiating in a ring beneath the head, each arcing outward and up before curling down toward the floor at varying radii, plus 2 longer feeding tentacles raised higher with clubbed tips — mixing some arms raised skyward with others sprawled along the ground, each built from 5-6 joint chains. I'm tallying the joint budget: roughly 48 for the eight tentacles, 14 for the feeding arms, plus spine, head, eyes, jaws, and fins, staying within the 160 limit and the 1000-part budget, with suckers along each tentacle's underside done via sweeps.

Now I'm estimating part counts per arm — tube segments, suckers, armor plates, and bands — aiming for roughly 20 parts per arm across 10 arms, plus mantle plating, ridges, eyes, and beak, landing near 400 parts total, while reminding myself to keep API usage conservative since there's no typechecking. I'm also establishing the coordinate convention, with the model facing +Z and tentacle azimuth angles defining each limb's direction in the XZ plane, and starting to define the root body joint and its role in the skeleton.

Now I'm building the mantle joint chain parented to the pelvis, running a catmull path from the body base up to a tip point with named spans so the chain tapers correctly, and I'm shaping the mantle as a teardrop sweep with a radius profile that widens near the middle and narrows to a point, mimicking an octopus's bulbous body.

For the head, I'm placing a large flattened ellipsoid tilted back near the top of the mantle, facing forward-down, and considering whether to model it as its own joint aimed toward a forward-down target so the geometry orients naturally.

For eyes, I'm thinking cephalopod-style with glowing orange horizontal slit pupils against dark teal lids, built from a dark outer sphere plus an emissive orange iris cap and a dark pupil box, possibly using a decal texture instead of separate geometry pieces.

Writing SVG eye texture...

Now I'm shaping the head as an ellipsoid positioned in front of the mantle, with the mantle itself as the main body mass and brow ridge plates layered over the eyes.

For the beak, I'm setting up a jaw joint hinged to the head, with upper and lower beak pieces built from swept curved paths tapering to a point, positioned where the arms converge at the front-bottom of the body.

Now I'm working out the tentacle attachment ring—placing roots for eight arms evenly spaced around a center point beneath the mantle, with azimuth angles spreading them radially while keeping rear arms tucked under the body's underside.

I want the body to sit up higher so it reads as rising out of the water, supported by the tentacles beneath, so I'm raising the overall body center upward. Then I'm defining each tentacle's path parameters—reach distance, peak height, tip lift, curl, and lateral sway—sampled at several points along the arm's length to shape its curve.

For arms that stay raised, they arch up and curl at the tip, while for arms that reach the floor, they rise from the base, arch outward, descend to the ground around the two-thirds mark, then trail along the floor with the tip curling upward. I'm tapering the tentacle radius from thick at the base to thin at the tip, and making sure the floor-bound arms' height matches the tube radius so they appear to rest naturally on the ground rather than sinking through it.

Now I'm working out the joint chain structure for each arm — using a seven-point spline so I get six spans plus a curling tip joint, which keeps each arm around seven joints. Counting up all the arms (short ones plus the two long ones) gives roughly 90-some joints total, comfortably under the 160 limit, and I'm deciding the parent joint for each chain should default to the nearest existing joint, likely the pelvis.

For color, I'm thinking through an Overwatch-style palette with a deep blue-teal body, a lighter cream underside, and orange accents, and weighing whether to use crisp cel-shaded toon paint versus a softer painted look for that clean color-blocked read.

Calculating texel density for the painted surfaces: mantle and tentacles total roughly 100 m², so a 1024 paint size gives about 1.2 cm per texel, which is workable, but I'll bump to 2048 for safety and use a 4096 atlas overall.

Now I'm settling on a color palette: deep and light blue for the hide, cream for the belly, white-grey armor plates with navy trim, and a single bold orange accent to keep the overwatch silhouette readable.

Still defining mantle colors and countershading...

For the arms, I realize a single countershade paint handles belly-versus-back coloring automatically based on surface orientation, so tentacle undersides naturally read as cream where they curve downward. I'm now placing suckers along the underside of each arm sweep using cylinder sticks at the 180-degree angle.

I'm thinking of giving suckers glowing orange rims around darker cream centers, maybe using a torus for the outer ring, though sharing a glow material across many small parts to keep it manageable.

But that multiplies into way too many parts, so I'm reconsidering a simpler two-part version per sucker, or even better, using a flat card decal with a sucker texture drawn on it so each sucker is just one part lying against the surface instead of built from separate geometries.

Cylinder UV mapping would stretch a radial drawing badly on the sides, so a single-texture approach won't work cleanly—better to stick with the 2-part construction. I'm leaning toward keeping the glow confined to the rim only, with cream suckers and orange rim trim instead of full orange, and moving on to designing the sci-fi armor bands for the tentacles.

Planning cuff-style armor rings placed at intervals along each tentacle using sweep operations along the chain, with radius slightly larger than the tube to form raised bands, plus thinner trim rings in a contrasting color layered at the cuff edges.

For each arm, three cuffs mean six meshes total, leaving suckers placed only in the gaps between cuffs — I'm sketching out specific t-ranges for cuffs versus sucker zones along each tentacle.

Tallying it up: roughly 220 sucker meshes per arm across ten arms plus 60 cuff meshes, landing around 550 total elements, well under the 1000 budget, so I can even loosen sucker spacing slightly for a cleaner look near the tapering tip.

Each sucker's size is scaled to the local tube radius, oriented along the surface normal to seat flush and sink partially into the arm, built from a small tapered cylinder. I'm now defining the radius taper function per arm, with a thicker base radius for the main arms versus secondary arms, narrowing smoothly down to a thin tip.

Thinking about tip styling: whether to add a distinct accent color near the very tip of each arm, using a comparison against the default coat color to decide where the accent band applies.

Now I'm defining the arm paths — 8 base arms spread radially plus 2 longer raised feeding tentacles, using a generic function that computes radial distance and height along each arm's curve based on style (ground vs raised).

I'm shaping the arch tentacles to rise from the base, peak around u~.3-.4, then descend toward the floor by u~.75, curling the tip back upward near the end, while making sure the radius at each point stays above a minimum thickness so the tip doesn't vanish.

I'm checking that the lowest sweep of each tentacle just grazes the floor without dipping below it, accounting for the tube's radius and possible catmull-rom overshoot between control points, so I need to nudge the y-values near the floor-touching segment slightly higher to stay safe.

For the raised-arm pose, I'm designing a pair of arms that sweep upward and curl toward the sky, giving them an ascending y-sequence through the control points so they read like hands reaching up, while also adding a lateral sway offset perpendicular to the arm direction for a more natural curling silhouette.

Defining the arm layout...

Settling on 8 ground arms spread at various azimuths plus 2 raised tentacles that curl upward and sideways like claws, bringing the total to 10 arms before working out joint counts.

Now I'm defining the mantle's body chain geometry — setting the root points at the pelvis and tracing a curved spine upward through several waypoints with shrinking radii, aiming for the mantle to sweep roughly 2.8 units long toward the tip.

I'm placing the eyes forward near the head's front and letting the head blend into the mantle. The arms should emerge from beneath the head around a ring near the head's base, positioned so the creature appears to rise above the water line holding its arms upward, with the arm tubes rooted inside the head/mantle volume for a seamless join.

With eight arms spaced around a ring of radius 0.5 and each arm tube at radius 0.36, the chord between adjacent roots is only about 0.38, well under the arm diameter, so they'll overlap heavily and form a dense, lobed crown around the beak rather than distinct separate arms -- which actually reads fine as a cephalopod arm skirt but I should double check whether that's the look I want.

I'm reconsidering the beak placement, since at ring center it ends up swallowed by the overlapping arm bases with barely any clearance, so I want to widen the ring radius to around 0.75-0.78 and shrink the arm base radius so there's an open hole in the middle for the beak to actually show, then I'm checking how far that ring sits relative to the head's underside curvature to make sure the arm roots are still anchored naturally into the head rather than floating below it.

Now I'm positioning the beak itself as a hooked curve hanging from the jaw joint, sweeping forward and down then curling back under like a parrot's beak, using a tapering radius along a Catmull-Rom path for the upper mandible and a shorter counterpart for the lower one.

I'm also checking that the beak doesn't collide with the front arms, since both occupy the forward lower-face region — the beak tip reaches further out in z than the arm bases, so it should remain visible without being swallowed by the arm geometry.

I'm now plotting the arm curves outward from the shoulder, defining ρ and y coordinates at successive parameter steps to shape the arch from torso to ground.

Checking the arch's peak height against head position, the arms rise slightly above the head's center before curving down, with radius tapering along the length. I'm adding per-arm variation—scaling the arch height randomly and introducing lateral sway so each arm looks distinct rather than symmetric.

Working out the raised feeding-arm pose now, defining tip curl and the point sequence along each side so the arms reach up and inward naturally.

Still plotting arm coordinates... now I'm shaping the feeding tentacle, tapering its stalk radius from base to a thinner neck before widening into the club shape near the end.

Adjusting the club end to round with radius 0.12, then placing orange suckers along the club's inner face at angles 150-210 degrees spaced every 0.04 in t. Now moving to mantle details, starting with lateral cephalopod fins near the mantle top like a squid's arrowhead fin.

Working out fin geometry...

Finishing the fin outline with smoothing and bevel, then deciding on colors—leaning toward cyan-teal fins with radiating orange rib stripes painted procedurally based on angle from the root, keeping the orange accent modest rather than dominant.

Figuring out where the fin root attaches to the mantle tube is trickier than expected—since the tube runs upward and tilted back, I need to work out which side counts as the "dorsal" clock position for sampling the sweep, so I'll just compute the fin root directly from the mantle chain point instead of reasoning through the clock-angle convention.

I'll sidestep the import issue by defining my own closed-form radius function for the mantle rather than relying on the sweep module's interpolate helper, shaping it as a teardrop profile using a sine curve that tapers based on position along the tube.

Working out the mantle chain geometry and fin root placement, computing the point and tangent on the chain at t=0.55 and sketching where the outline curve should span vertically relative to that root.

For the fin's local axes, I want x perpendicular to the tangent for proper orientation, and I'm picking x=[s,0,0] since the tangent has zero x-component there, guaranteeing orthogonality. I'm also figuring out which bone or joint on the mantle chain the fin should attach to near that t value.

Now I'm thinking about the mantle's armor plating -- sci-fi style grey panels with ridge rings sweeping around sections of the mantle chain, plus a dorsal crest strip running along the top using repeated plate segments.

I need to figure out which side of the tilted mantle tube is actually facing "up" in world space, since the tube leans back about 30 degrees. Working out the tangent and perpendicular vectors to find the correct normal direction for placing the dorsal plates on the upward-facing side.

I'm checking the mantle's tangent in the lower section too, confirming the tilt is around 23° from vertical with the world-up still projecting forward. So the countershading logic seems off: an upright mantle with the back tilted rearward would end up painting the dorsal side cream instead of the belly, which is backwards from what I want for a rising kraken viewed head-on.

Let me rethink the mantle paint entirely—rather than fighting the normal-based countershade math, I think a simpler approach works better: keep the mantle mostly blue and mottled, skip the cream front band idea, and instead add white armor-plate accents for visual interest.

For texture I want scattered glowing orange dots as bio-luminescent accents across the mantle, like small light-emitting spots—maybe two dozen tiny glowing spheres placed via scatter, filtered to the appropriate normal range.

Now I'm planning mantle armor: ring cuffs at a few points along the body plus spine ridge plates toward the rear, using a manual loop over sweep frames since the built-in helper only samples the dorsal angle. For the rear plates, I'll shape tapered boxes that scale larger toward the base.

For the plate styling, I'm going with a crisp white-grey Overwatch-style armor look, adding orange stripe accents and dark navy underlay panels. I'm considering generating a small SVG panel texture with outlines, bolt details, and an orange chevron to apply across each plate face for added detail.

Adding cuff-specific color logic...

Now I'm planning the head and brow armor: a sphere for the head with coat-painted texture, plus plate-style brow shields extruded over the eyes for added facial armor detail.

Computing the surface intersection confirms the eye sits at z≈1.15, protruding slightly. I'm working out the outward normal direction from the ellipsoid gradient to orient the eye sphere and iris disc properly on the head's curvature.

Trying a flat disc for the iris creates a gap at the rim since the sphere curves away faster than the disc radius allows, so instead I'll use a partial sphere cap with stretched UV mapping for the iris texture to keep it flush against the eyeball surface.

Decal returns a Part so glow should work on it fine. For the eye itself, I'm thinking dark navy eyeball sphere with a glowing orange iris decal covering most of the surface, giving that cephalopod look with a horizontal slit pupil.

For the eye bezel, I'm adding a white armor torus ring positioned around the eye socket facing outward to frame it. Then I'm setting up the head bone and joint hierarchy -- head joint parented to pelvis with forward orientation toward the face, and jaw joint parented beneath head.

I'm skipping the funnel/siphon tube since peers suggested removing it, though I'll add eyeL and eyeR joints parented to head for rigging purposes without specific roles. For the mantle, I'm keeping the pelvis root joint with a "spine" role for the chain, and now I'm working out the water base and splash geometry using lathe outlines with appropriate radii to match the arm reach.

Still shaping the water geometry...

I'll scatter droplets loosely around radius 1.5-5.5 and heights 0.3-2.5 without worrying much about overlap with arms, since small spheres intersecting tentacles will mostly be invisible. For the water dish floor, I need to check that arm tips (reaching up to ρ=4.0 from center) stay within the water radius of 5.7, which centers around z=0.45.

Overall creature height runs about 8-11m given the mantle tip at 4.5 and raised claws at 5.5 with a ±4 spread -- scale feels right for a kraken. Now I'm working out the mantle armor plates, which I'll build as extruded shapes with rounded hex outlines and beveled edges, computing the local frame (normal, tangent, binormal) at each point along the mantle sweep so the plates face outward correctly.

Positioning the plates slightly embedded into the surface with a thin orange chevron stripe layered just above each one for detail. I'm planning around 12 plates total, and considering a panel-line paint pass for extra texture but may skip it to keep things simpler.

I'll build a plate helper that takes a sweep point with its position, normal, and tangent, computing the bitangent via tangent-cross-normal, then defining an octagonal hex outline using width and length offsets for the plate silhouette, layering a navy base with a smaller beveled white top plate and orange accent.

For the accent I'm defining a chevron-shaped polygon pointing upward, checking it forms a simple non-intersecting outline before placing these plates onto a curved tube surface sized appropriately for the mantle area.

Now mapping out plate placement: a rear row of six spine plates along the mantle's back, plus two symmetric side rows of four plates each at mirrored angles — giving fourteen plates per part, forty-two total across the three parts. I'll skip adding cuffs on the mantle itself and instead focus armor elsewhere.

For the mantle, I'm sketching collar sweeps near the base in white with a thin orange trim line, and a glowing orange "beacon" tip near the far end using a slightly oversized secondary sweep to create a glow effect, watching out for z-fighting overlap between the layers.

Now I'm thinking through the body's joint structure, starting with the pelvis as root and branching out to head, jaw, mantle chain, and arms.

Arms need a tentacle role in their chain options, and I'm working out naming for each arm segment -- six numbered joints plus a tip joint, making sure every joint name stays unique.

Setting up the skeleton imports, checking I'm only pulling in what's actually used from the builder, math, path, toon, glow, paint, texture, and sweep modules. Writing paint color combos...

Still layering mantle texture...

For the head I'll countershade from mantle to a lighter belly tone for soft gradient transition, and use the same approach for the arm coloring. Now I'm writing the cuff paint function that builds a banded structure with navy trim and an orange center stripe.

I'm also setting up cel-shaded armor paints that resolve nested paint objects based on surface normals, letting shading paints return other paints recursively.

I'm working out cuff geometry — radius bumps along the arm sweep with flat caps to create a chunky, bevel-like rim at specific t ranges. For the sucker placement, I'm using angle 180 on the arm sweep to orient features toward the underside rather than the dorsal-facing side.

Tracing the roll continuity through the arch: since orientation is parallel-transported from the starting reference, the outer-top surface of the arch stays dorsal throughout the curve, while the inner underside stays ventral — so placing suckers there correctly puts them facing into the curl, matching real anatomy.

Now for the sucker geometry itself, I'm building each as a two-layer cylinder: an orange rim slightly embedded into the surface, with a cream/navy pad nested inside, giving the bump-and-dimple look of a real sucker.

Now I'm budgeting the sucker geometry per arm to keep the part count reasonable — two torus-plus-cylinder parts per sucker, spaced roughly every 0.07 along each arm while skipping cuff overlaps, bringing the total across ground and raised arms to around 200 parts.

Tallying everything up: arms, suckers, cuffs, mantle, plates, fins, glow dots, head, water effects, droplets, beak, eyes, and head armor land around 480 parts total, which feels like a good target. I'm also considering adding small dorsal spikes along each arm for extra detail, maybe eight per arm, to give the ridge a more textured look.

Now I'm thinking about adding a glowing orange tip bulb to each arm tip, using a separate sweep segment for the last bit of the arm so it can glow independently from the main tube, keeping things simple without extra banding.

For the head, I'm considering a crown of three white armor horn plates between the eyes, using surface hit-testing around the head's center to place cone spikes at specific angles, with a helper function to handle cases where the surface query returns null.

For the brow ridges, I'm planning a swept armor rod with varying radius along a curved arc above each eye, computing the arc endpoints in head-local coordinates from the eye center and its surface normal to shape an inner-to-outer brow ridge.

For the brow sweep I'll drape a rough path onto the surface with a slight lift and a thin sweep radius, trusting the drape function to handle the curvature, and plan to reuse it for other decorations like a war-paint stripe. For eye placement, rather than computing geometry manually, I'll find the nearest surface hit to an approximate target point and use its position and normal to orient the eye.

Now I'm setting up a helper that asserts a surface hit isn't null, throwing a clear error if it is, so I can safely place eyes using azimuth and elevation around the head center. Then I compute the eyeball center by offsetting slightly along the surface normal from that hit point.

I'm defining the eye decal, projecting it onto the eyeball sphere using the normal direction with a small size and segment count for the texture grid.

Writing SVG code...

Skip emblem logos, but I'll add a decal of glowing orange bio-circuit line patterns on the mantle sides as a tribal-style accent, computing placement via surface hit points at specific azimuth and elevation angles.

Writing SVG decal code...

I'm thinking through how to extrude helmet plates using a helper that takes position, normal, tangent, and bone references, so plates like the head crest or mantle inherit rigid weighting from the nearest joint rather than full bone hierarchy.

I'll import the Frame type from the frame module and use its axis and at properties to build the plate helper, computing normal and tangent vectors for positioning.

Still writing plate helper...

Now I'm working through the mantle sweep's tangent getter and how to compute tangent directions for head plates using projected vectors, flattening them against the surface normal at each hit point.

For cheek plates near the beak I'm placing two symmetric pieces at fixed azimuth and elevation offsets, with a dark interior sphere for the mouth cavity.

For the beak itself, I'm tying the upper beak sweep to the head bone and the lower beak sweep to the jaw bone so they articulate independently, then setting up a color banding function for the upper beak with dark graphite tones and an orange tip accent.

Now I'm plotting the actual curve points for both beak pieces using catmull-rom splines through several control points, shaping the upper beak to hook back slightly and the lower beak to be shorter with a tapered radius profile along its length.

Adjusting the beak point coordinates...

Then I'm adding a hidden dark mouth interior sphere tucked under the head, and considering a small ring of teeth-like cone spikes around the beak to satisfy the creature's teeth requirement.

I realize when a ring item has no bone, its geometry attaches to the nearest joint by default, so I should anchor the line explicitly to the jaw joint for stability rather than relying on inferred bone assignment from a literal frame point.

I'm trying to pin down what `moved` actually expects—whether numbers represent local axis offsets versus model-space directions, and worrying that passing a frame-derived point back through `moved` could double-apply the transform. The semantics feel ambiguous enough that I need to check against the sample code's usage pattern to settle it.

I worry that treating Vector3 as an offset would double the position, so maybe I should pass `bone` explicitly instead, using `f.bone` (the heaviest joint) and falling back to the nearest joint if none exists.

For rings, I need a Frame rather than a raw Joint, so I'm considering explicitly passing `bone: jaw` for teeth since callbacks don't auto-pass bone, and figuring out how `ring()` builds its frame from a point and direction.

Confirming spike() works with a RingItem frame as both base and direction source, matching the existing library examples.

Now I'm moving into the arm path generation, defining an ArmSpec type with azimuth, reach, arch, and sway parameters, then writing a groundPath function that computes an array of 3D points using trig based on the azimuth angle...

Still writing groundPath...

Total arm length comes out around 4.3-5 meters, which seems reasonable. I'm tapering the ground arm radius so it's thicker at the base and narrower near the tip, with the very tip getting a small orange glow and curling upward smoothly into its final position.

Checking floor clearance at various points along the curve to make sure the arm radius doesn't let it clip through the ground, especially near the lower-middle and base sections where the curve dips closest to y=0.1.

Now I'm checking whether the rear arms, positioned at azimuths around 125-160 degrees, might intersect the mantle geometry since their trajectory passes close to the mantle's z-range and radius at that height.

Checking the rear arm root position confirms it sits inside the mantle's lower cap, which is fine for exit geometry. I'm reconsidering shifting the mantle's path slightly back and shrinking it to clean up the silhouette, adjusting pelvis and torso waypoints accordingly.

Finalizing the mantle curve points gives a total length around 3.0 with about a 25° tilt from vertical, and the pelvis joint coincides with the chain's starting joint, which is fine since overlapping joints don't cause issues. I also need to check that the head ellipsoid sits properly within the front surface of the mantle given their relative z-positions.

I'm now verifying that the mantle joins cleanly with the head's top point, checking the eye positions relative to the head center using azimuth and elevation angles, placing the beak between the head's lower bounds, confirming the arm ring center coordinates, and starting to trace the raised arm path as it extends laterally from the body.

Working out the raised arm curve points and checking they don't collide with the lowered ground arms near the crown, then beginning to define the club radius function at the arm's base.

Now I'm placing suckers along the raised arm stalk and club, with a tighter column near the base and three wider columns clustered near the tip, scaling their size by the radius function. I'm also working through the dorsal orientation as the arm curls from outward-and-up near the base toward inward at the tip, tracking how the top-facing side rotates along that path.

I'm adding dorsal spikes spaced evenly along the arm's top centerline, sized relative to the local radius, and sketching out their color as a pale armor tone.

Now I'm scattering glowing orange sphere accents across the mantle surface, keeping them spread apart with a minimum distance filter and embedding them slightly into the surface for a built-in look.

Then I'm shaping the water mound base with a lathe profile, defining the outline points that'll create its rounded contour.

Writing ripple ring geometry...

For the splash crown, I'm placing 14 water-spike cones leaning outward from the mound's base, colored pale foam-blue, plus 26 droplet spheres scattered around for extra texture.

Now I'm thinking about the water disc's floor contact, attaching all the water parts to the pelvis bone so they move loosely with the body. For the fins, I'm calculating their root position along the mantle at roughly t=0.62, spanning outward about 1.25 units with a slight downward droop.

Shaping the fin outline...

Now I'm figuring out the fin coloring—a light teal base with darker navy ribs fanning out from the root at angular intervals, plus an orange rim band near the outer edge.

Attaching the arm joint to the mantle bone chain, then building the tube sweeps for arms with appropriate radius functions and side counts for a rounded low-poly look. I'm working out how the sucker points attach along the arm sweep, using bone weights so the skin bends naturally with the frame.

Adding cuffs as separate sweeps with a slightly wider radius and flat caps, reusing the same radius function so it stays consistent with the arm shape. Now I'm thinking through naming and grouping for the sweeps before moving on to glow effects on the eyes and other dot elements.

I need to make sure glow only targets flat-colored materials rather than baked paint, since glow on paint-baked parts could break -- so decals and emissive dots should use plain hex colors or textures, and glow will clone per material to keep things safe across orange sticks and tattoo decals.

I'm skipping extra tentacle details and instead polishing the fins and arm cuff: the cuff gets a flat orange stripe (not glowing), the beak gets a flat orange tip band, and I'm adding fin joints hinged off the mantle for a fan-like rig, positioning the fin root bone appropriately.

Now I'm defining eye joints parented to the head, aiming outward, and setting up the mantle as a spine chain built from a Catmull-Rom spline through four points, with four matching bone names for the spans plus tip. I'm also working out the parent hierarchy -- head off pelvis, jaw off head, and arms rooted near the pelvis despite sitting visually close to the head.

Setting up the arm chains now...

Confirming all imports are used, then setting up the metadata with name, description, style, and commit hash before moving on to the palette definition.

Defining the hide color with mottled and spotted shading for the skin texture.

I'm defining the belly tone and layering countershading paints for the arms and head with different gradient levels, plus setting up solid armor, navy, and orange color variants. I'm also considering whether the mantle needs its own stripe treatment or just inherits the hide paint directly.

Defining the mantle radius profile...

Still building skeleton joints...

Adding mantle collar cuffs near the base and a glowing tip sweep near the top, then setting up a plate extrusion helper for the armor loops.

Still sorting out imports...

Stacking plate layers so the chevron sits proud above the top plate without exceeding bevel limits, then placing these armor plates along the mantle by sampling tangent points from the sweep curve at each spine position.

I'm now sizing the rear and side rows of plates, deriving width and length from the mantle radius function at increasing t-values so they taper smoothly, and checking the side rows don't collide with the fin positions near the clock's lateral sweep.

For the mantle decals, I'm placing tattoo markings on both flanks using azimuthal lookups around the mantle surface, sized and oriented so they sit naturally on the curved sides. Writing decal placement code...

I'm now checking the vertical position against the fin geometry, since the fin's y-span at that point along the mantle path seems to overlap the decal zone -- I may need to shift the decal lower or raise the fin's attachment point to avoid the conflict.

There's a slight overlap between the fin root and decal edges around y 3.15-3.8, so I'm nudging the decal size and angle smaller to minimize it, accepting a minor crossing since it's not significant enough to fully resolve.

Now I'm working out eye placement from the skull surface hit, plus head-top and cheek plates using directional raycasts against the ellipsoid head surface, and starting to figure out how the brow drape should follow a polyline path.

Working through the ellipsoid intersection math to find the exact brow placement point along the direction vector from head center.

The brow should sit just above the eyeball like a heavy lid, which checks out with the geometry. I'll use the drape function with a catmull path for the brow, then add a crest of small cone-shaped horns near the forehead between the brows.

Now I'm setting up the eye joints on both sides symmetrically, naming them eyeL and eyeR based on mirrored offsets from the head surface. For each eye I'm building a dark sphere for the eyeball plus an armor-colored torus bezel ring around it to frame the socket.

Adding a glow decal on the eyeball surface, projecting along the normal direction from the offset point, double-checking the projection origin sits correctly on the sphere.

I realize the decal grid size could clip past the eyeball's silhouette at the corners, so I'm shrinking it to 0.36 to keep points within the sphere radius. Now moving on to the mouth, beak, and teeth ring geometry.

Now I'm placing a ring of cone-shaped teeth around the jaw, tilted and radiating outward from the beak so they sit mostly hidden within the lower head mass. Starting on the arms next.

Defining cuff bands, ground and club taper radii, and a reusable makeArm function that builds a catmull-rom chain parented to the pelvis and sweeps a tube mesh along it.

I'm adding cuff rings with flat caps and color painted by position, a glowing orange tip for ground arms, and starting on sucker placements for the club arms.

Still writing sucker geometry...

The pad sits partly under the ring, which looks fine as a cream disc with an orange ring, but I think a dark navy center reads better as a sucker mouth against the orange, so I'll switch to that for contrast. Now moving to the dorsal spikes...

Writing spike geometry code...

I'm also adding a foam ring at the arm's floor contact point, placing a flattened torus near the base to suggest cushioning where it touches the ground.

Now I'm sketching out naming and angle specs for each ground-contact arm around the body—front, side, back, and tail positions at roughly 22°, 58°, 125°, and 160° offsets—to keep the leg placement systematic.

Setting each arm's sway value individually for variety while keeping the rig symmetrical overall, then double-checking that neighboring arms with different angular offsets won't intersect given their reach and curvature. Next I'm moving on to building the sucker chains along each arm, then placing scattered droplet spheres at randomized angles and radii around the scene.

Writing water lathe geometry and ripple ring placements...

Checking the overall bounding box stays within y=0 and the water radius, nothing dips below the surface. Moving on to the tattoo SVG and eye texture next, and double-checking for unused imports.
